newsitem.title: USA: UPS, striking Teamsters talk past midnight, recess.
newsitem.headline: UPS, striking Teamsters talk past midnight, recess.

text.p: United Parcel Service and union officials took a break early on Friday from marathon talks aimed at ending a costly 12-day-old strike and agreed to resume discussions later in the day amid signs that they might be getting closer to a contract deal.
Dave Helfert, spokesman for the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, said both sides needed to analyze data and do complex mathematical computations before talks could continue.

"There are some serious numbers to be crunched. It's going to take several hours. When the work is done, they will reconvene," Helfert told reporters at the Capitol Hill hotel where the two sides launched their third attempt to end the strike just after 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) on Thursday.
He said the talks were "substantive and detailed" and described the mindset of the negotiators, who are meeting with the help of a federal mediator, as "tired and determined."
The strike by 185,000 UPS sorters, loaders and drivers -- one of the biggest U.S. work stoppages in the last 25 years -- began Aug. 4 and UPS says it is costing $300 million a week in lost business.

Union and company negotiators agreed to take a break and rest at around 1:45 a.m. EDT (0545 GMT) after nearly 17 hours of talks billed by both sides as informal. But the mood at the Capitol Hill Hyatt was better than during previous talks.

"The fact that they are crunching numbers tells me they are dealing in detailed issues," said Helfert, when asked if the talks had moved into the realm of formal negotiations. "There are plans to continue talking when they have this data."

Efforts to end the strike, one of the biggest U.S. work stoppages in over a quarter century, appeared to be moving forward after signals from UPS Chairman James Kelly on Thursday that the company might be more open to compromise.

Teamsters President Ron Carey remained in Washington, cancelling a speech at an Atlanta union rally, while Labor Secretary Alexis Herman scrapped her scheduled trip to Alabama. All the parties remained in the hotel.
But officials were far from predicting a deal was imminent, and Kelly was not present at Thursday's talks.

Kelly had declared the dispute at an impasse on Wednesday, but earlier on Thursday struck a more conciliatory note on pensions and on whether UPS's "final" offer was open to change under the right conditions.

"There is no one or two single issues that will determine whether we're able to reach agreement," he told news agency reporters in a telephone interview from Atlanta, although UPS later objected to reports it said over-interpreted Kelly's remarks.
Kelly said that the latest round of talks could eventually lead UPS to drop its final offer.
"If those informal discussions lead us to believe that the negotiations could be concluded at some point in time, then the last, best and final offer would cease to exist," he said.

In a statement, UPS later stressed it had not changed its offer and again urged the union to let its members vote on what it has called its "last, best and final offer." UPS said it hoped the ongoing discussions would "prove to be fruitful."

Issues include the union's desire to add more full-time jobs and UPS' plan to set up a new pension fund to cover only UPS workers and replace the existing fund, covering union workers at dozens of companies, mostly trucking lines.
The strike has crippled the nation's largest package delivery company and sent thousands of businesses scrambling to find other ways to ship their goods.

The U.S. Postal Service estimated on Thursday it was getting 15 percent to 20 percent of the 12 million daily packages which usually move on UPS volume. It said it hired more than 4,000 temporary workers to cope with the added volume.
